source: The intensity of treatment required for cure varies substantially among subsets of children with ALL. Risk-based treatment assignment is used in children with ALL so that patients with favorable clinical and biological features who are likely to have a very good outcome with modest therapy can be spared more intensive and toxic treatment, while a more aggressive, potentially more toxic therapeutic approach is reserved for patients with a lower probability of long-term survival. Certain ALL study groups, such as the Children’s Oncology Group (COG), use a more- or less-intensive induction regimen based on a subset of pretreatment factors, while other groups give a similar induction regimen to all patients.
target: For children with a poor response to treatment who are not in remission after remission induction therapy, further treatment is usually the same treatment given to children with high-risk ALL.
section: Treatment options for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia

source: CML is a clonal panmyelopathy that involves all hematopoietic cell lineages.
target: CML often begins in an early myeloid blood cell when a certain gene change occurs.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: For more information about TAM and MLDS, see Childhood Myeloid Proliferations Associated With Down Syndrome Treatment.
target: TAM is a disorder of the bone marrow that can develop in newborns who have Down syndrome.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: CML is caused by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, a translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (i.e., t(9;22)) resulting in fusion of the BCR and ABL1 genes.
target: This makes a very short chromosome 22 (called the Philadelphia chromosome ) and a very long chromosome 9. An abnormal BCR-ABL gene is formed on chromosome 22.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: For more information, see Childhood Chronic Myeloid Leukemia Treatment. Other chronic myeloproliferative neoplasms, such as polycythemia vera, primary myelofibrosis, and essential thrombocytosis, are extremely rare in children. For more information, see Childhood Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia Treatment.
target: This summary is about the treatment of childhood AML, transient abnormal myelopoiesis, childhood acute promyelocytic leukemia, juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, childhood chronic myelogenous leukemia, and childhood myelodysplastic syndromes. For information about the treatment of childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia, see Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: Maintenance chemotherapy is no longer part of pediatric AML protocols because two randomized clinical trials failed to show a benefit for maintenance therapy when given after modern intensive chemotherapy. Contemporary APL therapy also does not use maintenance chemotherapy.
target: The treatment of childhood APL includes a third phase called maintenance. The goal of maintenance is to kill any remaining leukemia cells that may regrow and cause a relapse.

source: Granulocytic sarcoma (chloroma) describes extramedullary collections of leukemia cells.
target: Myeloid sarcoma is also called granulocytic sarcoma or chloroma.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: The risk of t-AML or t-MDS depends on the treatment regimen. It is often related to the cumulative doses of chemotherapy agents received and the dose and field of radiation administered.
target: Cancer treatment with certain chemotherapy drugs and/or radiation therapy may cause therapy-related AML (t-AML) or therapy -related MDS (t-MDS). The risk of these therapy-related myeloid diseases depends on the total dose of the chemotherapy drugs used and the radiation dose and treatment field.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: Additionally, early recovery marrows in any of the subtypes of AML may be difficult to distinguish from persistent leukemia, although the application of flow cytometric immunophenotyping and cytogenetic/molecular testing have made this less problematic.
target: The myeloblasts, or leukemia cells, in AML are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: While the t(15;17) fusion that results in the PML:: RARA gene product is defined as a pediatric AML risk-defining lesion, given its association with acute promyelocytic leukemia, it is discussed in Childhood Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia.
target: The PML-RARA gene sends a message that stops promyelocytes (a type of white blood cell) from maturing. The promyelocytes (leukemia cells) can build up in the blood and bone marrow so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets.
section: General Information About Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Other Myeloid Malignancies

source: For information about the treatment of children with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), see Childhood Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia Treatment.
target: These drugs are used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia.

source: The development of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) or myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) after treatment with ionizing radiation or chemotherapy, particularly alkylating agents and topoisomerase inhibitors, is termed therapy-related AML (t-AML) or therapy-related MDS (t-MDS).
target: If the MDS becomes acute myeloid leukemia (AML), treatment will be the same as treatment for newly diagnosed AML.

source: Individuals with immunodeficiency have an increased risk of Hodgkin lymphoma, although the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma is even higher.
target: Low-risk Hodgkin lymphoma requires fewer cycles of treatment, fewer anticancer drugs, and lower doses of anticancer drugs than high-risk lymphoma.

source: For more information, see the Treatment of Recurrent Classic HL section in Hodgkin Lymphoma Treatment.
target: Recurrent Hodgkin lymphoma is cancer that has recurred (come back) after it has been treated.

source: The risks to the heart are related to the amount of radiation delivered to different depths of the heart, volume and specific areas of the heart irradiated, total and fractional irradiation dose, age at exposure, and latency period.
target: For male survivors who received radiation therapy to the chest, there may be a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

source: More than 90% of pediatric anaplastic large cell lymphoma cases have a chromosomal rearrangement involving the ALK gene.
target: In many children, anaplastic large cell lymphoma is marked by changes in the ALK gene that makes a protein called anaplastic lymphoma kinase.
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies anaplastic large cell lymphoma as a subtype of peripheral T-cell lymphoma.
target: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a type of lymphoma that mainly affects T-cell lymphocytes.
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: Other types of lymphoma, such as the nonanaplastic large cell peripheral T-cell lymphomas (including T/NK lymphomas), cutaneous lymphomas, and indolent B-cell lymphomas (e.g., follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma), are more commonly seen in adults and rarely occur in children.
target: There are two general types of lymphomas: Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: These include involvement of lymph nodes and a variety of extranodal sites, particularly skin and bone and, less often, gastrointestinal tract, lung, pleura, and muscle.
target: It usually forms in the lymph nodes, skin, or bone, and sometimes forms in the gastrointestinal tract, lung, tissue that covers the lungs, and muscle.
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: The World Health Organization (WHO) classifies lymphoblastic lymphoma as the same disease as ALL.
target: Lymphoblastic lymphoma is a lot like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: For more information about the tumor biology and genomic alterations, see the Tumor Biology (Genomics of anaplastic large cell lymphoma) section.
target: A pathologist checks for these cell and gene changes to help diagnose anaplastic large cell lymphoma.
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: Involvement of lymph nodes, usually above the diaphragm, may be a prominent feature. There may also be involvement of bone, skin, bone marrow, central nervous system (CNS), abdominal organs (but rarely bowel), and, occasionally, other sites such as lymphoid tissue of Waldeyer ring, testes, or subcutaneous tissue.
target: Lymph tissue is also found in other parts of the body such as the stomach, thyroid gland, brain, and skin.
section: General Information About Childhood Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma

source: The other three patients relapsed with primarily classical Hodgkin lymphoma histology and required treatment with salvage therapy.
target: Recurrent non-Hodgkin lymphoma is cancer that has come back after treatment.

source: Treatment of patients with MALT lymphoma of the gastric mucosa may also include antibiotic therapy, which is considered standard treatment in adults.
target: Antibiotics have been used to treat mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. Treatment with antibiotic therapy has been mostly studied in adults.

source: For information about the treatment of adults, see Mycosis Fungoides and Other Cutaneous T-Cell Lymphomas Treatment.
target: It may also be used to treat cutaneous T-cell lymphoma ( mycosis fungoides ).

source: Primary cutaneous lymphomas are now thought to represent a spectrum of disorders, distinguished by clinical presentation. Because of the rarity of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, no standard treatments have been established. Management and treatment of patients with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma should be individualized and, in some cases, watchful waiting may be appropriate.
target: Steroid therapy that is applied to the skin is used to treat cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

source: Neuroblastoma originates in the adrenal medulla and paraspinal or periaortic regions where sympathetic nervous system tissue is present (see Figure 1 ).
target: Neuroblastoma often begins in the nerve tissue of the adrenal glands.

source: Findings from epidemiological studies have not unequivocally linked environmental or other exposures to increased or decreased incidences of neuroblastoma.
target: There are many risk factors for neuroblastoma, but many do not directly cause cancer.

source: When neuroblastoma occurs in this age range, it shows a more indolent clinical course than neuroblastoma in younger patients, and it often shows de novo chemotherapy resistance. Neuroblastoma in adolescents and young adults may also exhibit unusual clinicopathological characteristics such as large tumors, bilateral adrenal disease, and pheochromocytoma-like features.
target: In children with a gene mutation, neuroblastoma usually occurs at a younger age, and more than one tumor may form in the adrenal glands or in the nerve tissue in the neck, chest, abdomen, or pelvis.

source: For more information, see the Genomic and Biological Features of Neuroblastoma section. Using the Therapeutically Applicable Research to Generate Effect Treatments (TARGET) and genome-wide association study data sets, a study compared the genomic and epigenomic data of primary diagnostic neuroblastomas originating in the adrenal gland (n = 646) with that of neuroblastomas originating in the thoracic sympathetic ganglia (n = 118). Neuroblastomas arising in the adrenal gland were more likely to harbor structural DNA aberrations such as MYCN amplification, whereas thoracic tumors showed defects in mitotic checkpoints resulting in hyperdiploidy.
target: Neuroblastoma is a type of cancer that forms in neuroblasts (immature nerve tissue) in the adrenal glands, neck, chest, or spinal cord.

source: Radiation therapy has become part of the standard of care for patients with high-risk disease and is usually delivered after high-dose chemotherapy and stem cell rescue.
target: High-dose chemotherapy and radiation therapy with stem cell rescue

source: Approximately one-half of all newly diagnosed patients with neuroblastoma have non–high-risk disease (i.e., low and intermediate risk).
target: For neuroblastoma, the stage of disease affects whether the cancer is low risk, intermediate risk, or high risk.

source: Presence of IDRFs has been associated with an increase in intraoperative complications, incomplete tumor resection, and worse survival in numerous studies.
target: IDRFs are used to determine the risk of surgery and the chance of completely removing the tumor.

source: As a result, published results from clinical trials for patients with non–high-risk neuroblastoma from the past used different staging systems (International Neuroblastoma Staging System) and response criteria or protocol-specific response criteria, making it difficult to compare trial results.
target: The results of some tests and procedures used to diagnose neuroblastoma may be used for staging.

source: For more information, see the sections on Treatment of High-Risk Neuroblastoma and Treatment of Recurrent or Refractory Neuroblastoma in Neuroblastoma Treatment.
target: Refractory neuroblastoma is a tumor that does not respond to treatment.

source: For example, in the case of spinal cord compression, an IDRF is present when more than one-third of the spinal canal in the axial plane is invaded, when the leptomeningeal spaces are not visible, or when the spinal cord magnetic resonance signal intensity is abnormal.
target: IDRFs are found on MRI or CT scans done during diagnosis.

source: Clinical trials are appropriate for these patients and may be offered.
target: For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be an option.

source: Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy have been considered the standard of care for Ewing sarcoma.
target: In Ewing sarcoma of bone, the cancer most often spreads to the lung, other bones, and bone marrow.

source: The observation that high-dose therapy with autologous stem cell rescue improved outcomes for patients with a poor response to initial therapy in the EURO-EWING-INTERGROUP-EE99 study must be interpreted in this context. The advantage of high-dose therapy as consolidation for patients with a poor response to initial treatment with a less intensive regimen cannot be extrapolated to a population of patients who received a more intensive treatment regimen as initial therapy. Extraosseous Ewing sarcoma is biologically similar to Ewing sarcoma arising in bone.
target: Stem cell transplant is used to treat localized and recurrent Ewing sarcoma.

source: Adequate local control for metastatic sites, particularly bone metastases, may be an important consideration. Multidrug chemotherapy for Ewing sarcoma always includes vincristine, doxorubicin, ifosfamide, and etoposide. Most protocols also use cyclophosphamide and some incorporate dactinomycin.
target: Chemotherapy for Ewing sarcoma is taken by mouth or injected into a vein.

source: Appropriate imaging studies of the suspected primary site are obtained before biopsy.
target: The selection of the biopsy site is important.

source: For more information about diagnostic biopsy, see the Treatment Option Overview for Ewing Sarcoma section.
target: Tests and procedures to detect, diagnose, and stage Ewing sarcoma are usually done at the same time.

source: The pathologist is consulted before biopsy/surgery to ensure that the incision will not compromise the radiation port and that multiple types of adequate tissue samples are obtained.
target: A biopsy site that is not properly selected may result in more extensive surgery to remove the tumor or a larger area that is treated with radiation therapy.

source: Thyroid cancer incidence is higher in children aged 15 to 19 years (34.4 cases per 1 million people), and it accounts for approximately 14% of all cancers arising in this older age group.
target: Although thyroid cancer can affect children of all ages, it's more common in adolescents and girls.

source: A retrospective analysis identified factors associated with bilateral thyroid involvement in 115 pediatric patients with well-differentiated thyroid cancer.
target: Talk with your child's doctor if you think your child may be at risk for thyroid cancer.
section: Causes and risk factors for childhood thyroid cancer

source: Total thyroidectomy also optimizes the use of radioactive iodine for imaging and treatment.
target: Radioactive iodine is used because only thyroid cells take up iodine.
section: Tests to diagnose childhood thyroid cancer

source: Pheochromocytomas and extra-adrenal paragangliomas arise from neural crest tissue. Neural crest tissue develops into sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglia.
target: Paragangliomas form in nerve tissue in the adrenal glands and near certain blood vessels and nerves.
section: General Information About Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma

source: For more information, see the Treatment of Metastatic Pheochromocytoma section.
target: The disease is metastatic pheochromocytoma, not bone cancer.

source: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma characteristically form small nests of uniform polygonal chromaffin cells (“zellballen”). A diagnosis of malignancy can only be made by identifying tumor deposits in tissues that do not normally contain chromaffin cells (e.g., lymph nodes, liver, bone, lung, and other distant metastatic sites). In the absence of clearly documented metastases, no combination of clinical, histopathological, or biochemical features has been shown to reliably predict the biological behavior of pheochromocytoma.
target: After pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma have been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the tumor has spread to other parts of the body.

source: For more information, see the Treatment of Metastatic Pheochromocytoma section. Patients with inherited pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma are at risk of recurrent disease in the form of additional primary tumors. Follow-up evaluation and management of additional primary tumors in such patients is essential.
target: Different types of treatments are available for patients with pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma.

source: Several other chemotherapy regimens have been used in small numbers of patients, but the overall results were disappointing. Novel targeted therapies are emerging as potential treatment strategies for metastatic pheochromocytoma.
target: Systemic chemotherapy is used to treat pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas.

source: Chemotherapy has not been shown to improve survival in patients with metastatic pheochromocytoma; however, chemotherapy may be useful for symptom palliation. The best-established chemotherapy regimen is a combination of cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and dacarbazine (the Averbuch protocol).
target: Sunitinib, axitinib, and cabozantinib have been used as palliative therapy for metastatic and recurrent pheochromocytoma.

source: Operatively, parathyroid cancers may be distinguished from adenomas by their firm, stony-hard consistency and lobulation; adenomas tend to be soft, round, or oval in shape, and of a reddish-brown color.
target: Parathyroid cancer may be hard to diagnose because the cells of a benign parathyroid adenoma and a malignant parathyroid cancer look alike.

source: Conventional treatment with intravenous fluids, diuretics, and antiresorptive agents such as bisphosphonates, gallium, or mithramycin may help control the hypercalcemia.
target: Before surgery, treatment is given to control hypercalcemia.

source: In general, the clinical course and the gross pathology observed at surgery are as important as the histology to define a lesion as a parathyroid carcinoma.
target: Because parathyroid cancer grows very slowly, cancer that has spread to other parts of the body may be removed by surgery in order to cure the patient or control the effects of the disease for a long time.

source: The mean age at diagnosis is between 60 and 70 years; however, men of all ages can be affected by the disease. Because of delays in diagnosis, breast cancer in men is more likely to present at an advanced stage.
target: Men of any age can get breast cancer, but it usually occurs at a later age in men than in women.

source: Results in men have been similar to those seen in women with breast cancer. For more information, see the Surgical Treatment for Breast Cancer section in Breast Cancer Treatment.
target: Breast cancer is much more common in women, but men can get breast cancer because they also have breast tissue where cancer can start.

source: Male breast cancer is rare. Fewer than 1% of all breast carcinomas occur in men.
target: If you think you may have risk factors for male breast cancer, talk to your doctor.
section: What are risk factors for male breast cancer?

source: For men aged 25 years or older, or those who have a highly concerning physical examination, mammography is recommended as the initial test and ultrasonography is useful if mammography is inconclusive or suspicious.
target: Screening mammograms are not usually recommended for men, even those who are at increased risk of breast cancer. But your doctor may suggest staying alert to any changes in your breast or the skin of your breast and getting regular clinical breast exams.
section: What are risk factors for male breast cancer?

source: The approach to the treatment of men with breast cancer is similar to that for women.
target: Male breast cancer is usually treated in the same way as breast cancer in women.
section: How is male breast cancer treated?

source: Responses in men are generally similar to those seen in women with breast cancer. Breast conservation surgery with lumpectomy and radiation therapy has also been used and can be offered if standard criteria for breast conservation therapy are met.
target: However, men are more likely than women to have a mastectomy (surgery to remove the whole breast) rather than a lumpectomy (breast-conserving surgery) to remove the cancer because they have less breast tissue.
section: How is male breast cancer treated?

source: The approach to the treatment of men with breast cancer is similar to that for women. Because male breast cancer is rare, there is a lack of randomized data to support specific treatment modalities.
target: More research is needed to find better treatments for male breast cancer and to better understand differences between male and female breast cancers.
section: What is the survival rate and prognosis for men with breast cancer?

source: A study found that mortality after breast cancer diagnosis was higher in male patients than in female patients.
target: This may be because male breast cancer is often diagnosed at a later stage than female breast cancer.
section: What is the survival rate and prognosis for men with breast cancer?

source: PSA testing has increased the detection rate of early-stage cancers, some of which may be curable by local-modality therapies, and others that do not require treatment.
target: Studies are being done to find ways to make PSA testing more accurate for early cancer detection.

source: Survival depends on stage at diagnosis, and screening is assumed to identify some cancers at an earlier stage than without screening, leading to a reduction in mortality.
target: Cancer screening trials also are meant to show whether early detection (finding cancer before it causes symptoms ) helps a person live longer or decreases a person's chance of dying from the disease.

source: The fastest annual rate of decline occurred in men and women aged 65 years or older. There was a trend of increasing short-term incidence rates for individuals younger than 50 years in most population subgroups. Incidence rates of distal colon and rectal cancers decreased in men and women for all ages combined.
target: This decline was largely driven by falling rates in adults aged 65 and older, who continue to have the highest overall rates of colorectal cancer.

source: The potential physical harms of fecal-based testing include the same harms as for colonoscopy for people with a positive test who have been referred for diagnostic colonoscopy.
target: A positive test result may lead to more testing, including colonoscopy.

source: Potential harms are organized according to the type of harm (e.g., physical, psychological, and hassle/opportunity costs) and when they occur in the screening cascade (e.g., screening test/workup; screening test/workup results; surveillance and surveillance results; and early treatment and overtreatment). For example, potential harms of screening colonoscopy include harms of the screening test itself (e.g., perforation and bleeding), results of the screening test (e.g., anxiety from an abnormal result), surveillance (e.g., harms of more frequent colonoscopies), and treatment (e.g., earlier treatment or overtreatment).
target: Different screening tests have different risks or harms.

source: Autopsy studies suggest that a significant number of individuals die with lung cancer rather than die of lung cancer.
target: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in the United States.

source: These studies illustrate possible improvements for determining the population of patients who may benefit the most from screening, potentially reducing the number of false positives and reducing the potential harm related to the adverse events associated with their evaluation.
target: Scientists study screening tests to find those with the fewest harms and most benefits.

source: There have been intensive efforts to improve lung cancer screening with newer technologies, including low-dose computed tomography (LDCT). LDCT was shown to be more sensitive than chest radiography.
target: The trial used chest x-rays or LDCT scans to check for signs of lung cancer.

source: Younger individuals and those without a significant risk of lung cancer may be more likely to suffer a radiation-induced lung cancer from screening than to be spared a lung cancer death.
target: Younger people and people at low risk for lung cancer are more likely to develop lung cancer caused by radiation exposure from screening than to be spared death from lung cancer.

source: False-positive exams may result in unnecessary invasive diagnostic procedures. Based on fair evidence, some of the lung cancers detected by screening chest x-ray and/or sputum cytology appear to represent overdiagnosed cancer; however, the magnitude of overdiagnosis is not clear.
target: Screening test results may appear to be normal even though lung cancer is present. A person who receives a false-negative test result (one that shows there is no cancer when there really is) may delay seeking medical care even if there are symptoms.

source: Neither study observed a reduction in lung cancer mortality with screening.
target: Finding lung cancer may not improve health or help you live longer.

source: A systematic review of the benefits and harms of computed tomography (CT) screening for lung cancer summarized 21 studies with respect to various diagnostic outcomes, although not all studies reported on all outcomes.
target: Talk to your doctor or other health care provider about your risk for lung cancer, whether a screening test is right for you, and about the benefits and harms of the screening test.

source: For a complete description of factors associated with an increased or decreased risk of ovarian cancer, see the Factors With Adequate Evidence of an Increased Risk of Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers section in Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers Prevention.
target: Different factors increase or decrease the risk of getting ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancers.
section: General Information About Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers

source: Ovarian cancer is rare; the lifetime risk of being diagnosed with ovarian cancer is 1.12%.
target: Although ovarian cancer is rare, it is the sixth-leading cause of death from cancer in women.
section: General Information About Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers

source: TVU (or transvaginal sonogram [TVS]) has been proposed as a screening method for ovarian cancer because of its ability to reliably measure ovarian size and detect small masses.
target: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVU) to screen for ovarian cancer has not been shown to decrease the number of deaths from the disease. TVU is a procedure used to examine the vagina, uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and bladder.
section: Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers Screening

source: Gynecologic examination usually includes a manual pelvic examination, but this procedure is commonly viewed as lacking sensitivity for detection of early-stage disease. There is no evidence of the benefit of this test for the early detection of and decreased mortality from ovarian cancer, so it is not further considered.
target: Pelvic exams to screen for ovarian cancer have not been shown to decrease the number of deaths from the disease. A pelvic exam is an exam of the vagina, cervix, uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and rectum.
section: Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers Screening

source: Based on solid evidence, screening for ovarian cancer results in false-positive test results. Screened women had higher rates of oophorectomy and other minor complications such as fainting and bruising.
target: A false-positive test result can also lead to an unneeded oophorectomy (removal of one or both ovaries ).
section: Risks of Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers Screening

source: These tests are often performed in combination. Several biomarkers with potential application to ovarian cancer screening are under development but have not yet been validated or evaluated for efficacy in early detection and mortality reduction. A U.S.
target: Problems caused by tests used to diagnose ovarian cancer include infection, blood loss, bowel injury, and heart and blood vessel problems.
section: Risks of Ovarian, Fallopian Tube, and Primary Peritoneal Cancers Screening

source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common malignant neoplasm worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer deaths in men and women combined in the United States. It is estimated that there will be 154,270 new cases diagnosed in the United States in 2025 and 52,900 deaths caused by this disease. Between 2012 and 2021, incidence rates for CRC in the United States declined by about 1% per year overall.
target: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer death in the United States when numbers for men and women are combined. Between 2012 and 2021, the number of new colorectal cancer cases in the United States decreased.

source: Incidence and mortality rates are higher in Black individuals than in those of other races; however, a meta-analysis found no evidence that Black individuals have higher rates of precancerous lesions.
target: Studies show that Black people are not more likely than others to have precancerous growths.

source: For most people, the major factor that increases a person’s risk for colorectal cancer (CRC) is advancing age. Risk increases dramatically after age 50 years; 90% of all CRCs are diagnosed after this age.
target: The risk of colorectal cancer increases after age 50.

source: Five studies have reported a positive association between alcohol intake and colorectal adenomas.
target: Drinking alcohol is also linked to the risk of forming large colorectal adenomas (benign tumors).

source: Celecoxib reduces the incidence of adenomas; however, celecoxib does not have a clinical role in reducing the risk of sporadic CRC.
target: Studies have shown that taking the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug celecoxib reduces the risk of colorectal adenomas (benign tumors) coming back after they have been removed.

source: No relationship was found between cigarette smoking, even smoking of long duration, and recurrence of adenomas in a population followed for 4 years after initial colonoscopy. A meta-analysis of 106 observational studies found a RR (ever smokers vs. nonsmokers) for CRC incidence of 1.18 (95% CI, 1.11–1.25), with an absolute risk increase of 10.8 cases per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 7.9–13.6).
target: Cigarette smokers who have had surgery to remove colorectal adenomas are at an increased risk for the adenomas to recur (come back).

source: The investigators found the effect of calcium was similar across age, sex, and baseline dietary intake categories of calcium, fat, or fiber. The study was limited to individuals with a recent history of colorectal adenomas and could not determine the effect of calcium on risk of the first adenoma, nor was it large enough or of sufficient duration to examine the risk of invasive CRC. After calcium supplementation is stopped, the lower risk may persist up to 5 years.
target: It is not known if taking calcium supplements lowers the risk of colorectal cancer.

source: Most case-control studies of cigarette exposure and adenomas have found an elevated risk for smokers.
target: Smoking cigarettes is also linked to an increased risk of forming colorectal adenomas.

source: Based on fair evidence, removal of adenomatous polyps reduces the risk of CRC. Much of this reduction likely comes from removal of large (i.e., >1.0 cm) polyps, while the benefit of removing smaller polyps—which are much more common—is unknown.
target: It is not known if removing smaller polyps lowers the risk of colorectal cancer.

source: Epithelial cancers in the lung appear to develop in a series of steps extending over years.
target: Lung cancer is a disease in which malignant (cancer) cells form in the tissues of the lung.

source: The most important risk factor for lung cancer (and for many other cancers) is cigarette smoking.
target: Tobacco smoking is the most important risk factor for lung cancer.

source: Based on solid evidence, taking vitamin E supplements does not affect the risk of lung cancer. Magnitude of Effect: Strong evidence of no association.
target: Studies show that taking vitamin E supplements does not affect the risk of lung cancer.

source: Cigarette smoking is the most important contributor to the lung cancer burden because of its high prevalence of use and because cigarette smokers tend to smoke frequently, but cigar and pipe smoking have also been associated independently in case-control and cohort studies with increased lung cancer risk. The cigar risks are of particular concern because of the increased prevalence of cigar use in the United States.
target: Cigarette, cigar, and pipe smoking all increase the risk of lung cancer.

source: Compared with nonsmokers, smokers experience a dose-dependent increase in the risk of developing lung cancer (and many other malignancies). Approximately 85% of all lung cancer deaths are estimated to be attributed to cigarette smoking. Substantial benefits accrue to the smoker by quitting smoking.
target: In smokers who have been treated for lung cancer, quitting smoking lowers the risk of new lung cancers.

source: Studies of dietary factors have yielded intriguing findings, but because the diets of smokers tend to be less healthy than those of nonsmokers, it is challenging to separate the influence of dietary factors from the effects of smoking.
target: However, since smokers tend to have less healthy diets than nonsmokers, it is hard to know whether the decreased risk is from having a healthy diet or from not smoking.

source: Based on equivocal evidence, the observed inverse associations between lung cancer and dietary factors, such as fruit and vegetable consumption, are difficult to disentangle from cigarette smoking.
target: Some studies show that people who eat high amounts of fruits or vegetables have a lower risk of lung cancer than those who eat low amounts.

source: Based on solid evidence, long-term sustained smoking cessation results in decreased incidence of lung cancer and of second primary lung tumors.
target: In a person who has quit smoking, the chance of preventing lung cancer depends on how many years and how much the person smoked and the length of time since quitting.

source: In nonsmokers, important lung cancer risk factors are exposure to secondhand smoke, exposure to ionizing radiation, and occupational exposure to lung carcinogens, such as asbestos.
target: Avoiding risk factors and increasing protective factors may help prevent lung cancer.

source: The Reduction by Dutasteride of Prostate Cancer Events (REDUCE) trial randomly assigned 8,231 men aged 50 to 75 years at higher risk of prostate cancer (i.e., PSA 2.5–10.0 ng/mL) with one recent negative prostate biopsy to dutasteride at 0.5 mg daily or to placebo.

target: The types of treatment your child may receive depend on whether the congenital hemangioma will shrink on its own.

source: There is no standard treatment for epithelioid hemangioma because it has not been studied in clinical trials.
target: Hemangiomas of this type go away over time without treatment.

source: These hemangiomas are mostly fully formed at birth and are characterized by telangiectasia and venules with light and dark areas of skin coloration (see Figure 2 ). They resolve spontaneously and are pathologically GLUT1 positive. They are mainly located on the lower body but can be present in the head and neck area.
target: It most commonly appears on the skin on the head and neck. Hemangioma may be a single lesion, one or more lesions spread over a larger area, or multiple lesions in different parts of the body.

source: In several studies, ultrasonography evaluations have failed to identify some spinal abnormalities that were later found on MRI evaluation. Infants with more than five hemangiomas need to be evaluated for visceral hemangiomas. The most common site of involvement is the liver, in which multiple or diffuse lesions can be noted.
target: If the hemangioma is part of a syndrome, more tests, such as an echocardiogram, MRI, magnetic resonance angiogram, and eye exam, may be done.

source: In addition to pain control, management includes steroid ointments, antibiotic ointments or systemic antibiotics, laser therapy, or topical timolol. Most infantile hemangiomas occur sporadically. However, they may rarely be caused by an abnormality of chromosome 5 and present in an autosomal dominant pattern.
target: These symptoms may be caused by problems other than an epithelioid hemangioendothelioma. The only way to know is for your child to see a doctor.

source: Propranolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, is first-line therapy for infantile hemangiomas.
target: The beta-blocker propranolol is usually the first treatment for hemangiomas.

source: Propranolol therapy is usually used during the proliferative phase but has been effective in patients older than 12 months with infantile hemangiomas.
target: Infantile hemangioma may also be treated with propranolol and steroid therapy or propranolol and topical beta-blocker therapy.

source: There is no standard treatment for epithelioid hemangioma because it has not been studied in clinical trials. Treatment usually consists of curettage, sclerotherapy, or resection.
target: Sclerotherapy is used to treat epithelioid hemangioma.
section: Types of treatment for childhood vascular tumors

source: Topical beta-blockers are used mainly for the treatment of small, localized, superficial hemangiomas as an alternative to observation. They have also been used in combination with systemic therapy in complicated hemangiomas or to prevent rebound in hemangiomas being tapered off of systemic treatment.
target: Beta-blockers are drugs commonly used to lower blood pressure and heart rate, but they can also shrink certain types of vascular tumors, such as infantile hemangiomas. Beta-blocker therapy may be injected into a vein, taken by mouth, or placed on the skin ( topical ).
section: Types of treatment for childhood vascular tumors

source: There are many other published reports about the efficacy and safety of propranolol.
target: Propranolol is also used to treat benign vascular tumors of liver.

source: Smaller lesions may be found incidentally during surgery, radiological studies, or endoscopy. The natural history of these incidental tumors and the frequency of progression to symptomatic disease are unknown. There may be a substantial reservoir of small GISTs that do not progress to symptomatic stages.
target: Sometimes GISTs are smaller than the eraser on top of a pencil. Tumors may be found during a procedure that is done for another reason, such as an x-ray or surgery.

source: TKIs work by inhibiting aberrantly functioning KIT or PDGFRA receptor tyrosine kinases and inducing rapid reduction in tumor growth.
target: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are targeted therapy drugs that block signals needed for tumors to grow.

source: Other TKIs (i.e., sunitinib or regorafenib) may have some activity, but most patients are recommended to consider enrolling in clinical trials, if eligible. For more information on the efficacy, safety, and management of toxicity of imatinib, or additional agents in the setting of imatinib resistance or intolerance, see the sections on Treatment of Resectable Primary GISTs, Treatment of Unresectable Primary GISTs, and Treatment of Metastatic or Recurrent GISTs.
target: Imatinib mesylate and sunitinib are two TKIs used to treat GISTs. TKIs are sometimes given for as long as the tumor does not grow and serious side effects do not occur.

source: TKI therapy is indicated for patients with unresectable, borderline resectable, metastatic, or recurrent GISTs. It is also indicated as adjuvant therapy for patients with GISTs at high risk of recurrence.
target: TKIs may be used to treat GISTs that cannot be removed by surgery or to shrink GISTs so they become small enough to be removed by surgery.

source: Radiation therapy rarely has a role in the management of patients with GISTs. It may occasionally be used for palliation of painful metastases or for patients with unresectable bleeding tumors.
target: Radiation therapy is sometimes given as supportive care to relieve pain in patients with large tumors that have spread.

source: The goal of surgery is complete gross resection with an intact pseudocapsule and negative microscopic margins. Because GISTs are generally encapsulated and relatively less infiltrative than other malignancies, wide excision is not necessary.
target: If the GIST has not spread and is in a place where surgery can be safely done, the tumor and some of the tissue around it may be removed.

source: A formal staging system for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) is available from the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Staging Manual.
target: Tests that examine the GI tract are used to diagnose gastrointestinal stromal tumors.
section: General Information About Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors

source: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) appear to originate from interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) or their stem cell-like precursors.
target: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor is a disease in which abnormal cells form in the tissues of the gastrointestinal tract.
section: General Information About Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors

source: In long-standing cases, systemic lesions can develop along the gastrointestinal tract, in lymph nodes, and in other organs.
target: Over time, lesions may form in other parts of the body, such as the stomach, intestines, or lymph nodes.

source: The visceral lesions are generally asymptomatic and are most often discovered only at autopsy, though clinically, gastrointestinal bleeding can occur.

source: As many as 33% of patients with classic KS develop a second primary malignancy, which is most often non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
target: Most often, this second cancer is non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

source: Usually, superficial radiation beams, such as electron beams, are used. Some authors believe disease recurrence in adjacent untreated skin is common if only involved-field radiation therapy is used and claim better cure rates when extended-field radiation therapy is used. For low-voltage (100 kv) photon radiation therapy, 8 Gy to 10 Gy is given as a single dose or 15 Gy to 20 Gy is given over 1 week because solitary lesions control nearly 100% of local disease, but recurrence in adjacent areas is common.
target: Photon radiation therapy treats lesions with high-energy light. Electron beam radiation therapy uses tiny negatively charged particles called electrons.

source: The female urethra is largely contained within the anterior vaginal wall. In adults, it is about 4 cm in length.

target: In women and men, proximal urethral cancer usually has spread deeply into tissue.

target: Tamoxifen is one of a group of drugs called selective estrogen receptor modulators, or SERMs.

source: Women with inherited conditions such as Lynch syndrome, Cowden syndrome, and polycystic ovary syndrome have an increased risk of endometrial cancer.
target: Polycystic ovary syndrome (a disorder of the hormones made by the ovaries) and Cowden syndrome are inherited conditions that are linked to an increased risk of endometrial cancer.

target: Tamoxifen is used to prevent breast cancer in women who are at high risk for the disease.

target: Obesity is related to other risk factors such as high estrogen levels, having extra fat around the waist, polycystic ovary syndrome, and lack of physical activity.

source: TVU is used as a diagnostic tool to evaluate symptomatic women with vaginal bleeding.

source: In the setting of abnormal uterine bleeding, endometrial sampling has gained favor largely as an alternative to more invasive procedures such as fractional D&C. Several methods of biopsy exist (e.g., Pipelle, Tao Brush, and Uterine Explora Curette) to identify endometrial pathology. Although endometrial sampling has largely replaced D&C as the first choice in the evaluation of women with bleeding, issues of access to the endometrial cavity and sampling error limit the clinical significance of a negative result.
target: Endometrial sampling is commonly used to examine women who have abnormal vaginal bleeding.

source: Risks associated with false-positive test results include anxiety and additional diagnostic testing and surgery. Endometrial cancers may be missed on endometrial sampling and ultrasound.
target: A false-positive test result (one that shows there is cancer when there really isn't) can cause anxiety and is usually followed by more tests (such as biopsy ), which also have risks.

source: There is no standard chemotherapy for vulvar cancer, and reports describing the use of this modality in the setting of metastatic or recurrent disease are anecdotal. Extrapolating from regimens used for anal or cervical squamous cell cancers, chemotherapy has been studied in combination with radiation in the neoadjuvant setting or as primary therapy in advanced disease.
target: Topical chemotherapy for vulvar cancer may be applied to the skin in a cream or lotion. The way the chemotherapy is given depends on the type and stage of the cancer being treated.
